transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-11
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 51 minutes
Attendees: Priya Mehta (Redwood AE), Eli Navarro (Redwood SE), Marcus Li (Redwood Solutions Eng), Maya Chen (VP of ML, Solstice), Raj Patel (Infra Lead), Sofia Martinez (CISO), Andre Gomez (SRE)

Auto-generated summary (may be incomplete):
Solstice is evaluating Redwood Dedicated for production inference for a real-time recommendations product. Primary concerns: isolation for PII models, burst headroom for shopping launches, 99th percentile latency SLOs, and failover to hosted variants during capacity shortages. They requested pricing, SLA, and a technical deep-dive on KV cache and batch behavior.

Topics discussed:
- Current infra and why dedicated vs hosted
- Isolation and compliance (KMS, VPC, audit logs)
- Burst strategy and reserved vs burst capacity
- Autoscaling behavior, canary rollouts, and failover policies
- Monitoring and tracing (token-level costs, latency percentiles)
- Next steps and action items

Transcript body:
[00:00] Priya: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. Quick intros from our side — I'm Priya, AE on the account, and Eli's our SE. Marcus is joining for the infra-flows later.
[00:18] Maya: Hi, Maya here. I'm VP of ML at Solstice, leads the recommendations work.
[00:22] Raj: Raj, infra lead - I run our k8s clusters and cloud networking.
[00:27] Sofia: Sofia, CISO - I will flag security questions.
[00:30] Andre: Andre, SRE, day-to-day on capacity.
[00:33] Eli: Great, thanks. Quick agenda: understand your workload, constraints, and then map to Redwood Dedicated options — reserved pools, isolation, burst guardrails, and failover.

[02:05] Maya: To start, we're moving from a mixed approach. Right now the recommendations endpoint is served from a mix of in-house GPU jobs and a hosted inferencing provider. Costs are spiking during promo windows. We want predictable latency and tighter control over data residency for a subset of models that touch PII.
[02:37] Priya: Makes sense. When you say 'predictable latency', can you capture the 95/99 numbers you care about? Also, tell us about request size, sequence lengths — are these short queries or long context runs?
[03:01] Maya: 95th target is under 80 ms, 99th under 200 ms for our production endpoint. Most requests are short — under 128 tokens — but during personalization we sometimes stream longer contexts to the model offline. Typical QPS baseline is 1200 rps and we need to handle 3x to 5x bursts for Black Friday-like events.
[03:35] Raj: And we need isolation for two model groups: PII (customer PII) which must be isolated in a private VPC and encrypted with our KMS; and general personalization models that can live in shared pools but with reserved capacity.

[04:10] Eli: Ok so two-segment strategy looks sensible: a dedicated private pool for PII models (Private deployment or Dedicated with VPC?), and a shared dedicated pool with burst guardrails for personalization. Quick question on failover: if we can't meet latency because dedicated pool is full, do you want automatic failover to a hosted-compatible model or rate limiting?
[04:42] Andre: Ideally automatic fallback to a hosted variant for non-PII models; for PII models we can't failover to hosted. So we need guaranteed capacity for PII.
[05:05] Priya: Understood. So the hard SLOs are for PII — dedicated nodes with strict isolation and no external fallback. For personalization, we can accept fallback to hosted or canary down to a lower-capacity model.

[06:12] Sofia: Security checklist: SOC 2 Type II, SSO (SAML), RBAC, KMS integration, audit logs retention. We also need to know where logs and transcripts live for compliance — can we opt out of storing prompts?
[06:45] Marcus: Redwood supports VPC peering and Private control planes; we have KMS integrations and you can configure audit log retention. We also have an option to redact or not persist prompts at rest — but some telemetry for billing/trace is required.
[07:20] Sofia: Okay. Also need encryption in transit and at rest, HSM for keys ideally.
[07:35] Priya: We can provide a security pack with SOC 2 attestation, product sheets on KMS/HSM, and details on audit log retention. We'll attach that in the follow-up.

[08:10] Raj: Back to capacity — you mentioned reserved pools. How do those work for bursts? Can we pre-commit to N GPUs and then burst above that for a short window? How is pricing handled?
[08:30] Eli: Reserved pools are a committed quantity of GPU capacity — you get guaranteed nodes for your account, predictable throughput. For bursts you have two options: 1) pre-purchase burst credits or a burst band that allows you to exceed commit for limited time at a premium rate; 2) autoscale against a shared overflow pool with fair-share routing which might introduce higher tail latency.
[09:10] Raj: So for Black Friday we want hard headroom — say 3x baseline for 24 hours. We'd prefer to pre-purchase burst capacity rather than risk tail latency.
[09:26] Priya: That maps to reserved + burst credits. We'll show a pricing example later. Note that dedicated pools can be isolated at the node level so multi-tenant interference is minimized; we also support node segregation by tenant to provide stronger isolation.

[10:00] Maya: One concern is model versions — we must be able to pin a model version for the PII pool and roll forward with canary traffic. How do rollouts work?
[10:20] Marcus: We support version pinning, canaries, and automatic rollbacks based on latency or quality regression. You can define a rollout policy per route.
[10:36] Eli: To add, you can define fallback policies — if a canary fails we can automatically switch traffic to previous version or to a hosted-variant. For PII you would disable the hosted fallback.

[11:15] Andre: On caching — our offline jobs rely on a KV cache for prefix caching to speed up repeated requests. How is KV managed across dedicated pools? Is it local to a node or shared?
[11:36] Eli: Our KV cache can be configured either per-pool or per-node. For lowest latency, a local KV co-located with the GPU node is best; for consistency across replicas a shared distributed KV can be used, but that may add ms of latency. There's also the option for warmed prefix caches during flash sales.
[12:02] Raj: Any guidance on hit rate and memory sizing?
[12:10] Eli: Typical hit rates depend on request locality — for personalization, a 70% hit rate on top N keys is achievable with a small working set. We'll need your traffic histogram to recommend memory and shard counts.

[13:00] Maya: About failover again — if personalization fails to hosted fallback, would Redwood buffer requests or do backpressure? We don't want to drop recommendations but we also don't want to block upstream.
[13:22] Priya: We expose configurable policies: queueing/backpressure, graceful degradation (lower-capacity model), or immediate fallback. Each has unit cost tradeoffs and latency implications.

[14:05] Raj: Let's talk metrics. We need token-level cost visibility, per-route 95/99 latency, and per-token billing breakdown. How granular are the observability dashboards?
[14:27] Marcus: Console offers per-route, per-model dashboards, traces, and token-level cost. You can also export traces to your preferred APM.
[14:41] Sofia: What's retention on logs? We sometimes need 12 months for audit.
[14:49] Marcus: We have standard retention tiers and an enterprise retention add-on for longer windows. We'll include options in the security doc.

[16:00] Maya: Ok — timeline: we're aiming for a pilot in Q3 with production in Q4. For pilot we want a small dedicated pool for PII models and ability to route 10% of traffic to Redwood Dedicated to validate latency and cost. Any blockers from your side?
[16:22] Priya: Sounds feasible. We'll need the workload profile and network access details. For pilot we can provision a small isolated pool and run a smoke benchmark. We'll also need an NDA addendum for the pilot if there's any sensitive data.

[17:10] Andre: One weird constraint — our infra team uses long-lived gRPC connections and a custom request header for user context. Do you support sticky sessions or forwarding headers?
[17:28] Eli: Yes, we preserve headers and support sticky affinity by session or by client ID. gRPC streaming is supported in hosted and dedicated runtimes; you'll need to ensure the client TLS config matches Redwood's expectations.

[18:05] Raj: Network egress — if we run in VPC peering, we want minimal cross-AZ hops. Does Redwood guarantee region locality?
[18:20] Marcus: Yes, you can pick regions and we route requests to nearest nodes; private control plane options keep traffic within your VPC where possible. We'll map region placement during provisioning.

[19:00] Maya: For the pricing examples could you show committed vs on-demand token pricing and burst band pricing? Also show an example of reserved GPUs pricing per month and effective per-token cost at different utilizations.
[19:22] Priya: Absolutely — I'll attach a worked example. Expect both per-token tiers and GPU-reserved monthly rates and a burst premium. We'll run a simple model to show cost at 40%, 70%, and 95% utilization.

[20:10] Sofia: Are there penalties for underutilization on reserved pools? If we commit to N GPUs but only use at 30% we need visibility on reclaim or resizing options.
[20:25] Eli: Reserved contracts typically have term commitments with some resizing windows. We have quarterly rebalancing options and limited ability to scale down mid-term with a fee. We'll include contract terms in the pricing doc.

[21:05] Raj: For emergency scale, can we put an autoscale policy that pulls from a shared overflow and triggers a billed burst automatically? We need an SRE playbook for that.
[21:20] Marcus: Yes — autoscale policies can target dedicated pools first, then overflow shared pool, with rate-limits per route. We can provide an ops playbook and webhook hooks for alerts.

[22:00] Maya: For the pilot, what metrics should we surface to decide go/no-go? I'm thinking: 99th latency under 200ms, error rate <0.1%, cost per 1k tokens within 15% of target. Anything else?
[22:18] Priya: Those are good. Add model quality drift checks (we can plug in your evaluation set), and functional checks for RBAC/KMS.

[24:00] Andre: Can we run a simulated load test that mimics Black Friday spikes? How would Redwood handle pre-warm and KV warming?
[24:18] Eli: Yes, we can coordinate a load test. Pre-warm is supported by seeding KV caches and spinning up warm nodes. We'll share a load test plan and discuss network egress patterns to avoid throttles.

[26:00] Raj: About telemetry — we'd like to ingest Redwood traces into our internal SRE dashboards. Is there a native exporter?
[26:12] Marcus: We export to OTLP/Jaeger and can ship traces to your endpoint. Also token-level billing data can be exported to S3 or BigQuery.

[27:40] Sofia: Any responsibilities on our side we should be aware of? E.g., audit of prompts or PII handling?
[27:55] Priya: You'll be responsible for classifying PII models and managing keys; Redwood will provide tooling to enforce policies and audit. We'll include a checklist for security owners.

[29:10] Maya: One more thing — model quantization. We might want to use int8 or nf4 quantized variants to save cost. Does Redwood support quantized forks and do you guarantee same API?
[29:28] Eli: We support several quantization profiles. You can pin quantized variants per model and fallback to full precision if needed. Performance profiles are provided.

[31:00] Andre: Can we get a runbook for incident response — e.g., node failure, degraded latency, cache corruption?
[31:12] Marcus: Yes — we'll provide an operations runbook, playbooks for failover, and escalation contacts for enterprise customers.

[33:00] Maya: Is there a sandbox or testbed we can access to smoke the integration before the pilot?
[33:10] Priya: We can provision a time-limited test environment in our hosted sandbox or spin up a small dedicated test pool depending on contractual terms. For sensitive data we'd advise using the dedicated pool in your VPC.

[34:00] Andre: For the 3x burst for Black Friday, are there hard limits in the provider — like doubling only? I want to know the ceiling.
[34:12] Eli: There are physical limits per-region. If you need 3x sustained for N hours we'll recommend pre-provisioning or multi-region provisioning. We also have burst credits to cover short spikes.

[35:40] Raj: Let's talk SLA — what uptime % and latency SLO commitments come with Dedicated contracts?
[35:52] Priya: Dedicated contracts have SLA tiers — 99.9% and 99.95% etc. For latency we provide target latency bands and remediation credits for missed SLOs. We'll include the SLA matrix in the doc.

[37:00] Sofia: Regarding logs, can we do redaction at ingest for PII prompts?
[37:12] Marcus: Yes, redaction hooks are available; we can integrate with your redaction rules and ensure non-persistence of prompt text for certain routes.

[38:30] Maya: Okay, to wrap — what do you need from us to get the pilot moving?
[38:38] Priya: Four things: 1) workload profile (QPS, token distribution, seq length), 2) a small set of routes and models you want in PII pool, 3) network/access checklist for VPC peering, and 4) confirmation on pilot timeline and NDA terms.

[39:05] Raj: We'll get that over — expect the histograms and job schedules by Monday.
[39:12] Priya: Great. We'll also send an initial pricing example and the security packet.

[40:00] (brief side conversation about internal team availability, inaudible)

[41:20] Maya: One more technical nit — do you support GPU pinning for low-noise model inference? We have noisy neighbors concerns.
[41:32] Eli: Yes, node-level isolation and GPU pinning are available on Dedicated; we can reserve whole nodes for the PII pool.

[42:15] Andre: And how about deployment time — once we sign, how long to provision a dedicated pool?
[42:25] Marcus: Typical lead time depends on region and size — small pools can be provisioned in days, larger multi-node pools may take 2-4 weeks. We'll provide an expected provisioning timeline.

[43:00] Priya: Okay let's recap next steps — I'll send the pricing + SLA + security pack by Monday, Eli will prepare the batch/KV sizing questionnaire and schedule the deep dive, and Raj will share traffic histograms. Any adjustments?
[43:20] Raj: That matches our expectations.
[43:26] Sofia: Please also include the audit retention options.
[43:31] Priya: Noted.

[44:10] (short pause, few people typing)

[45:00] Priya: Final question — competitors. Are you evaluating others still?
[45:06] Maya: Yes, we have exploratory conversations with Vertex and a few self-hosted options. Cost and speed tradeoffs are the deciding factors.
[45:18] Priya: Understood. We'll make sure the pricing example is explicit about reserved vs on-demand tradeoffs.

[46:00] Andre: Can we get a small benchmark run — like 10k requests — to reproduce our 95/99 calculations? Even synthetic workloads help.
[46:12] Eli: Absolutely — we'll coordinate the synthetic trace and workload once we have the histogram.

[47:20] Maya: Great. If we get pilot green, what's the contracting cadence? Quarterly reserves or annual?
[47:30] Priya: We offer both. Many customers start quarterly and move to annual for discounting. We'll include both term options in the pricing doc.

[48:10] Sofia: Last security Q: pen testing windows — can we request a pen test of the managed control plane if needed?
[48:20] Marcus: Yes, we have a process for customer-initiated pen tests; we require scheduling and scope approval. We'll include the PSO contact.

[49:00] Priya: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up. Any final comments?
[49:08] Maya: No, that's it. Thanks.
[49:12] Raj: Thanks all.
[49:15] Sofia: Thanks.
[49:20] Priya: Great, we'll talk soon.

[50:00] (call ends)
